h: Authoritarians stumble in five countries, but India's road is harder
dek: According to Anand Teltumbde, voters from Hungary to the United States have defeated right-wing governments, but this is a reprieve, not liberation, and India's road is far harder.
body: In seven months, voters in five countries pushed back hard-right leaders in power. In Hungary, Orbán's 16-year rule ended; in Brazil, Lula defeated Bolsonaro's son; in Serbia, a students' list removed Vučić from power; in Israel, Netanyahu lost his majority; and in the United States, Trump's party lost both houses. Writer and civil rights activist Anand Teltumbde sees this as relief, but not as the defeat of the forces that stand behind these leaders.

As he sees it, these results share three things. People were angry about rising prices, corruption, unemployment and crumbling public services; young people gave the movements their edge, especially in Serbia, where the old parties stepped back and made room for the students; and enough life was left in electoral institutions for the votes to be counted correctly.

Hope has stirred in India too. A jibe at unemployed youth gave birth to the 'Cockroach Janata Party'; the paper leaks brought demands for the education minister's resignation; then the Chief Election Commissioner came under fire over the revision of the voter rolls; and on 1 November opposition parties came out together at the Ramlila Maidan.

But according to the writer, the road here is far harder. Hungary has about one crore (10 million) people; India has one billion four hundred million. What stands opposite is not just one party but the hundred-year-old network of the RSS. A 2023 law put the appointment of election commissioners almost entirely in the hands of the Centre, and the Supreme Court has avoided clashing with the executive. The opposition also has no shared blueprint of equal citizenship that rises above caste, religion and language.

So he lists three lessons: the movement needs a path to elections that is independent of parties yet effective; first, the credibility of elections must be restored, which calls for paper ballots for some time and full VVPAT checks; and after victory, the real work will be rebuilding broken institutions.
nazar: Teltumbde's most useful warning is that it is possible to win the streets and lose the election. In India this danger falls hardest on those whose names are most easily struck off the voter rolls: migrant workers, Muslims, Dalit and Adivasi (indigenous) settlements, and women without papers. The credibility of elections is not just an opposition issue; it is a question of whether the vote of the citizen on the margins exists at all.
His point is also worth remembering that in other countries the government changed, not the structure. In India too, if only the faces change, the promise of equality will stay unfinished.
sawal: How will India's young people build a path like Serbia's students did?
ref: VVPAT
A machine attached to the EVM that shows the voter, on a paper slip, whom the vote went to. There has long been a demand that all these slips be counted.
Cockroach Janata Party
A youth movement formed in response to a remark about unemployed young people. It has been protesting against the Election Commission since October 2026.
ank: Countries where authoritarians stumbled in seven months
The law on appointing election commissioners

h: Meitei-Naga closeness in Manipur opens a new rift, not peace
dek: An investigation by Scroll's Rokibuz Zaman shows that the shared demand to scrap the Kuki pact could bring deeper division, not peace.
body: On 31 October an unusual procession came out in Imphal. The Meitei body COCOMI and the Naga body United Naga Council marched together and demanded that the Centre cancel the 'Suspension of Operations' agreement with Kuki armed groups. Since 2023 both communities have been in separate conflicts with the Kukis. The killing of three Meitei men in Imphal East on 19 October, blamed on Kuki militants, was the immediate trigger for this coming together.

At least 300 people have been killed in the Meitei-Kuki violence that began in May 2023, and the state has been split almost in two. The Naga-Kuki conflict flared up from February 2026 and has so far taken 66 lives. At the root of the conflict is the Kuki demand for a separate administration for the hill districts, which both Meiteis and Nagas oppose.

According to the report, this friendship is limited to one demand. Naga leaders admit that the question of a greater Nagalim still stands between them, and a former Naga leader recalled that Meitei groups have long opposed the Sixth Schedule and more autonomy for the hills. The Kuki National Organisation calls it a bloc formed against it and flatly refuses to give up arms.

According to former Union Home Secretary G.K. Pillai, scrapping the agreement will not stop the violence as long as weapons remain in the hands of ordinary people. He blames the BJP governments at the Centre and in the state: no attempt was made at a political solution, the flow of arms was not stopped, and officers who cannot maintain law and order should step aside.
nazar: Manipur has been burning for three years, and Delhi's policy seems to be one of waiting. When two communities come onto one platform calling a third 'outsiders', the greatest danger is to the thousands of people in relief camps, women and children, whose return home gets pushed back again. The road to peace will not come from cornering one community, but from reducing everyone's weapons and everyone's fears.
sawal: When will the people in the relief camps be able to return to their villages?
ref: Suspension of Operations
A ceasefire agreed in 2008 between the Centre, the Manipur government and two Kuki armed groups. It expired in September 2026 and was not renewed.
Article 371C
A provision of the Constitution that gives Manipur's hill districts special protection and a separate committee in the assembly.

h: Tamil Nadu shuts its federalism committee: a U-turn by Vijay?
dek: According to former IAS officer M.G. Devasahayam, scrapping the Justice Kurian Joseph Committee is a retreat from the state's long fight for autonomy.
body: In six months as Chief Minister, C. Joseph Vijay has looked soft on the Centre. He stayed silent on the special revision of the voter rolls and on the opposition campaign to remove the Chief Election Commissioner. Former IAS officer and People-First chairman M.G. Devasahayam says this impression now seems confirmed, because on 6 November his government shut down the high-level committee on Centre-state relations.

Chaired by former Supreme Court judge Kurian Joseph, the committee was set up in April 2025, in the tradition of the Rajamannar Committee and the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions. Its first report, which came in February 2026, made big proposals: the Governor should be chosen from a list approved by the assembly and should be removable by the assembly itself; education should go back to the State List; NEET and the National Testing Agency should be abolished; English should become a permanent official language; and the decisions of the GST Council should be only advisory.

The report also rejected 'One Nation, One Election' and said the delimitation of seats should stay tied to the 1971 Census, so that states that brought down their population do not lose out. The second part was due by May 2027 and covered issues such as emergency provisions, river water disputes and Centre-state finances.

The government argues that the committee was set up only by a government order and that its work clashed with the State Law Commission. According to the writer, this argument does not hold, because the Law Commission is also set up by an order. He sees this in a time of growing centralisation by the Centre, and says that a retreat by Tamil Nadu, which has led the fight for federalism since 1962, is bad news for the whole constitutional structure.
nazar: Federalism is not a legal fine point. It decides what language a village child will study in, who will control medical admissions, and whether the state will have money left to spend on its poor. The burden of centralised exams like NEET has fallen hardest on students from villages and backward communities. A state shutting down its own committee halfway shows how fragile the fight for autonomy becomes as soon as power changes hands.
sawal: Who will write the second part of the Kurian Joseph Committee's unfinished report?
ref: Rajamannar Committee
A committee set up by the Tamil Nadu government in 1969 that made recommendations on Centre-state relations and state autonomy. It is seen as a milestone in the federalism debate.
Delimitation
The division of Lok Sabha and assembly seats according to population. Southern states fear that a new census will cut their seats.

h: The Arab vote that unseated Netanyahu, but the occupation stays
dek: According to Qassam Muaddi, Israel's Palestinian citizens blocked Netanyahu's path, but the camp taking his place is also against a Palestinian state.
body: After Israel's election last month, President Herzog has invited not Netanyahu but his main rival Gadi Eisenkot to form the government. Netanyahu's camp fell from 54 to 47 seats, and then a Haredi party also left him after failing to get a law exempting its community from army service. Qassam Muaddi, Mondoweiss's Palestine correspondent, sees Israel's Palestinian citizens as the real reason for this shift.

This population of about two million is roughly one fifth of the country's total. This time turnout was about 80 per cent, and two Arab lists won 19 seats for the first time, so neither big camp could reach the 61-seat majority. According to the writer, this was a response to the Gaza war, the crackdown on those who speak out, and talk by ministers like Smotrich of throwing Arabs out.

But the writer has no illusions about the opposition. As army chief, Eisenkot was responsible for the blockade of Gaza and is linked to the 'Dahiya doctrine' of disproportionate force against residential areas. Bennett, Lieberman and Golan also do not want a Palestinian state, and Lieberman prefers making a deal with the Haredim rather than with the Arab parties.

According to the writer, the new government may bring some small relief, such as the Palestinian Authority's withheld revenue, permits for workers and more aid into Gaza. But Eisenkot has promised to finish Hamas within 18 months, which could also mean bombing again.

His conclusion is that the basic picture will not change, but voting was still wise. If the danger of expulsion and mass killing falls even a little over the next four years, that is a big thing for the people of Gaza, the West Bank and Jerusalem.
nazar: This article shows that when a marginalised population votes together, it can overturn the arithmetic of a majority, even if it has no share in power. In India, Muslims and Dalits are often belittled as a 'vote bank', yet here we see that this very vote can decide how long a hardline government lasts.

The lesson is also that removing a leader and changing policy are two different things. When both the government and the opposition refuse to treat minorities as equal partners, democracy is reduced to a numbers game.
sawal: Why does no camp join hands with the Arab parties and their 19 seats?
ref: Dahiya doctrine
A military idea that came out of the bombing of Beirut's Dahiya district in the 2006 Lebanon war. It calls for deliberately using disproportionate force against residential areas.
Haredi
Israel's ultra-Orthodox Jewish community. Exemption from compulsory army service is a long-standing demand of their parties.

h: In Ethiopia, taking the capital is easy; keeping the peace is hard
dek: According to Mebratu Kelecha, after the military victory in Tigray, the real test is protecting ordinary people and delivering jobs and justice over land.
body: On 4 October federal forces entered Mekelle, the capital of Tigray, after TPLF fighters left the city. Twelve days later Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed set up a five-member interim administration, which has six months to rebuild institutions and prepare for elections. Independent researcher Mebratu Kelecha asks whether this victory will turn into peace.

The writer recalls that the 2022 Pretoria Agreement, brokered by the African Union, was sound on paper. It covered protecting civilians, restoring services and opening the way for aid. The weakness lay in carrying it out: Eritrea did not sign, and the Amhara armed groups and the TPLF factions were not bound to accept what their negotiators agreed.

Western Tigray is the sorest point. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty have documented the expulsion of Tigrayans there, and according to the report, restrictions on documents, movement, work and land still continue. This year the internal conflict in Tigray also grew, and in September seven groups, including the TPLF, Fano and the Oromo Liberation Army, announced an alliance to remove the Abiy government, even though their claims on the ground clash with each other.

On top of this, ties with Eritrea have broken down. Ethiopia has accused it of attacks and of helping rebels, which Eritrea denies, and Ethiopia's insistence on access to the Red Sea is a separate source of tension.

The writer sets four tests for peace: protection for every civilian, whichever side they are on; real livelihoods for fighters; supervised return home and return of land; and a real share for the people of Tigray in decisions on security and elections.
nazar: Ethiopia's story is not unfamiliar to India. Whether in Manipur, Kashmir or Bastar, the state here too often takes military control or a signature on an agreement to mean peace, while questions of displaced people's return home, land and jobs hang for years. The writer's four tests apply just as well to any internal conflict.
sawal: When will the people driven out of Western Tigray return to their land?
ref: TPLF
Tigray People's Liberation Front. The party that dominated power in Ethiopia for decades, and went to war with the federal government in 2020.
Pretoria Agreement
The ceasefire agreement between the Ethiopian government and the TPLF in November 2022, brokered by the African Union.

h: When clan and clout guard even the door to feminism
dek: According to Dr Rakhshinda Perveen, class discrimination in Pakistan is patriarchy's partner, and women themselves often become its gatekeepers.
body: The 16-day campaign against gender-based violence is set to begin on 25 November. Ahead of it, public health and gender expert Dr Rakhshinda Perveen raises an uncomfortable question: in the inequality we blame only on patriarchy, how big a part is played by class privilege and connections?

According to the writer, class in Pakistan is not just income. Family name, biradari (clan), tribe, domicile, accent, degree and closeness to powerful people all become unwritten qualifications that outweigh ability. Even a woman's rights are measured by her marriage, family, social circle and looks.

She says that when she raised the question of class in her university studies and in her organisation's work, she faced the most neglect from established elite feminists. Foreign donors and diplomats too keep relying on familiar names and well-connected middlemen. People from the margins are sometimes put forward only for show, but according to the writer, being visible is not power, and representation is not sharing.

The writer also refuses to accept that every woman who suffers patriarchy is automatically on the side of equality. In many organisations working on gender justice, the boards are elite, hiring happens behind closed doors, women do the work and the credit goes elsewhere. She makes it clear that missing out on a job is not the same as a poor woman's poverty and the violence she faces.

She calls for honest research into who gets appointments, recognition and protection, and for donors to examine their own hiring and partnership practices. According to her, fighting inequality while living comfortably on the privileges that inequality rests on is not feminism.
nazar: In India the same question becomes sharper with caste. Dalit and Adivasi (indigenous) women have said for years that mainstream feminism often runs on the experience of upper-caste, urban, English-speaking women, and that in the NGO world too the decision-making chairs stay with them. The writer's argument reminds us that representation must be counted at the level of boards and budgets, not just in the pictures on posters.
sawal: How many women on the boards of gender organisations come from working-class backgrounds?
ref: Intersectionality
The idea, put forward by legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw, that discrimination by gender, caste, class and race works together, not separately.
16-day campaign
An international campaign that runs every year from 25 November to 10 December and draws attention to violence against women.

h: Bangladesh's new cyber draft: a new name, the same fear
dek: According to Zillur Rahman, even after twelve amendments, jail terms for rumour and defamation could remain a tool to silence criticism.
body: To silence the media, you do not need to send every journalist to jail; a few cases are enough to frighten all the rest. Zillur Rahman, president of the Centre for Governance Studies, uses this idea to test the new draft of Bangladesh's cyber security law. The 2024 uprising raised hopes that this Sheikh Hasina-era method would end, but the writer has his doubts.

According to the report, the government made twelve changes to the draft after talks with civil society. To prove a rumour, it will now have to be shown that the statement was false; the punishment for defamation will be the same as in the 1860 Penal Code; and journalists cannot be arrested without the court's approval first. The writer sees these as good but insufficient steps.

Up to ten years in prison and a fine of up to forty lakh (four million) taka for spreading rumours remains as it was, and it is still the government and the police who will decide what is true and false. Yet reports of corruption or custodial deaths often rest only on informal sources. According to a study by his organisation and the Clooney Foundation, 396 journalists were caught up in 222 cases under the Digital Security Act between 2018 and 2023. In 30 cases examined in depth, 20 journalists began censoring themselves and three left the profession.

Sections 33 to 35, on search, seizure and arrest without a warrant, were not even touched. Notice after blocking is no substitute for prior court approval, and cancelling a whole organisation's licence over one person's conviction is excessive. Like Iftekharuzzaman of Transparency International Bangladesh, the writer also asks why protection is only for journalists, and not for the ordinary citizen.

A law on hacking, fraud or AI-generated abuse is needed, but according to the writer, protecting citizens from cybercrime and protecting the government from criticism are two different jobs. Only if criminal punishment for rumour and defamation is removed and court oversight is strengthened will this change be real.
nazar: This debate is not unfamiliar to India. Here too, in cases under the IT Act, the sections that replaced sedition, and the UAPA, convictions are few; the process itself becomes the punishment. The hardest blow falls on journalists and activists in small towns who write about Dalits, Adivasis (indigenous communities) or workers, and who have neither a big lawyer nor an institution behind them.
A split where the journalist is exempt and the ordinary citizen goes to jail is also dangerous, because today everyone who speaks on social media is reporting news in one form or another.
sawal: After cases against 396 journalists, why still ten years for a rumour?
ref: Digital Security Act (DSA)
Bangladesh's 2018 law under which large numbers of cases were filed against journalists and critics. In 2023 it was replaced by the Cyber Security Act.
The 2024 uprising
The student-led movement in Bangladesh after which Sheikh Hasina had to give up power and leave the country in August 2024.

h: 322 hate crimes in nine months, the state's hand in a third
dek: According to APCR's new tracker, 54 people were killed this year in attacks on Muslims and Christians, 21 of them at the hands of the police or army.
body: The Association for Protection of Civil Rights (APCR) released its hate crime and hate speech tracker on 10 November. According to The Wire's report, 322 hate crimes against Muslims and Christians were recorded across 24 states and Union Territories between 1 January and 30 September 2026. In 119 of these, a state agency was involved through its action or its silence, and in 81 the police directly.

These incidents took 54 lives. 21 deaths were at the hands of the police or army, 12 in alleged encounters and nine in custody or jail, yet not a single officer was charged in any of them. Of the 108 cases in which an FIR was filed, in 40 the case was instead filed against the victims themselves, and 21 of these are from Uttar Pradesh.

About 58 per cent of the incidents took place around festivals, the Kanwar Yatra and the Bengal election results, and meat or cattle was the most common pretext. The hate speech tracker records 83 speeches by 57 speakers, 33 of them by people holding constitutional or government posts, including five chief ministers or deputy chief ministers.

According to the report, the Supreme Court had told the police to register cases on their own without waiting for a complaint, yet only one such FIR was found in the whole year. APCR has acknowledged that about 60 cases are still to be verified and that the figures cover only reported incidents.
nazar: These figures show that the danger to minorities comes not only from mobs but also from the system that was meant to protect them. When the victim is the one charged and the people inciting from the stage are chief ministers, the rule of law stays on paper. In such a situation, the counts kept by citizens' groups are often the only record left.
sawal: Why is not a single officer in the dock for the 21 custodial deaths?
ref: APCR
Association for Protection of Civil Rights, a human rights organisation in Delhi. It documents hate crimes and provides legal help.
Suo motu FIR
The police registering a case on their own, without any complaint. The Supreme Court has said this is necessary in cases of hate speech.

h: Workers pay the bill for Delhi's toxic air
dek: When construction stops under GRAP, daily-wage workers lose their work, and the promised compensation of ten thousand rupees never reached many of them.
body: Every winter, as soon as Delhi's air turns bad, GRAP restrictions come in and construction work is the first to stop. According to Newslaundry's report, the hardest hit are migrant construction workers, who go without earnings for weeks or months, and many return to their villages with their children.

In its order of 24 November 2021, the Supreme Court had told the government to give financial help to workers affected by construction bans. In December 2025, Delhi minister Kapil Mishra announced compensation of ten thousand rupees for every such worker.

But workers said they had registered with the Delhi Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board about two years ago and renewed it on time, yet still did not get the money. The board says about one lakh (100,000) workers have been given about 100 crore rupees (1 billion), while its website lists 2.15 lakh (215,000) registered workers.

The workers' union Construction Workers Panchayat Sangam has filed an affidavit in the Supreme Court saying that about 1,700 workers are still waiting for compensation. The report has no direct response from the board or the government to these complaints.
nazar: Blame for pollution keeps going round between vehicles, industry and stubble burning, but the price is paid by the worker who carries bricks in that same toxic air and goes hungry when work stops. The welfare board holds money from a cess collected for the workers themselves; paying it out on time is no favour, it is their right.
sawal: Why are half of the 2.15 lakh registered workers left out of compensation?
ref: GRAP
Graded Response Action Plan: step-by-step restrictions imposed in Delhi-NCR according to air quality. At the higher stages, construction is banned.
Construction Workers Welfare Board
The board that manages the fund built from a cess on construction projects. It gives registered workers pensions, insurance and support.

h: Karnataka goes to the Supreme Court to save Dalit and Adivasi reservation
dek: The High Court had struck down the increase in the SC-ST quota; now the state government has filed a special leave petition.
body: The Karnataka government has filed a special leave petition in the Supreme Court against the High Court's ruling of 12 October. According to The News Minute's report, the Chief Minister's Office gave this information on 11 November. The High Court had struck down sections 3 and 4 of the 2022 law that raised the quota for Scheduled Castes from 15 to 17 per cent and for Scheduled Tribes from 3 to 7 per cent.

This increase had taken total reservation in the state from 50 to 56 per cent. The High Court said the state did not hold the required consultation with the national SC and ST commissions before making the law, and that letters sent later do not meet this condition. The law was made by the previous BJP government on the recommendation of the Justice H.N. Nagamohan Das Commission.

The present Congress government alleges that the BJP government made no serious attempt to get the quota placed in the Ninth Schedule. According to the government, the Centre told Parliament in March 2023 that it had received no such proposal, and in July 2026 put off a decision, saying the matter was pending in the High Court.

The state assembly passed a resolution on this in December 2025. In February 2026, recruitment for 56,432 posts was approved, in which the additional six per cent of posts for SC-ST candidates have been kept in the backlog until the court's decision.
nazar: When an increase in reservation gets stuck on a paperwork lapse, the loss falls on the Dalit and Adivasi (indigenous) young people who are waiting for these very recruitments. Both parties are blaming each other, but the Centre's silence, even though the Ninth Schedule route is open, is just as big a reason.
sawal: How long will the six per cent of posts in the backlog stay empty?
ref: Ninth Schedule
The list in the Constitution whose laws are hard to challenge in court. Tamil Nadu's 69 per cent reservation is in it.
Special leave petition
A petition under Article 136 asking the Supreme Court for permission to appeal against the decision of any court.

h: Visa cancelled for Norwegian journalist who questioned Modi
dek: Helle Lyng Svendsen, who was coming to speak on press freedom at the Bharat Summit in Hyderabad, says she was stopped just before her flight.
body: Norwegian journalist Helle Lyng Svendsen says the Indian government has cancelled her visa. She was to fly from Oslo to Hyderabad on Wednesday night, where she had a session on press freedom and democracy on 14 November at the Congress party's 'Bharat Summit'. According to her, she had both a visa and political clearance.

According to Svendsen, about ten minutes before she left for the airport, she got a call from the Indian embassy in Norway saying she could not travel. No clear reason was given. In a video she appealed directly to Home Minister Amit Shah to reverse the decision and said that, as she understood it, the decision was taken at the level of the Home Ministry. According to Navjivan, her claims have not been independently confirmed, and as of the morning of 12 November there had been no response from the government, the Ministry of External Affairs or the embassy.

The journalist herself lists several possible reasons: her question to Prime Minister Modi in Oslo on 18 May 2026 about why he does not take questions from the world's freest press, the video of which went viral; her articles on the Modi government's policies; her comments on Adani and Ambani; and her reporting on the 'Cockroach Janata Party'.

The two-day summit is being held at the initiative of Telangana Chief Minister Revanth Reddy and Salman Khurshid, with more than a thousand delegates expected from over 70 countries. Press Club of India president Sangeeta Barooah Pisharoty was also part of her session.
nazar: If the claim is true, the price of one question is a country's doors closing on a foreign journalist. The effect does not stop at the foreign media: when the government quietly blocks a visa, small journalists here, especially those who write about marginalised communities, understand how costly asking questions can be.
sawal: Why answer a question asked in Oslo by stopping a flight to Hyderabad?
ref: Bharat Summit
An international conference being held by the Congress in Hyderabad on 13-14 November. It has sessions on subjects such as democracy and press freedom.
Political clearance
Separate government permission needed for a foreign national to take part in a political event in India. It is required in addition to a visa.

h: FIR over anti-reservation posts, IIT Patna changes its registrar
dek: Professor Avlendra Thakur, accused over posts insulting Dalits, has given up the additional charge of registrar, and Dr Mahesh Kolekar has become acting registrar.
body: At IIT Patna, the registrar's work will now be handled by Dr Mahesh Kumar H. Kolekar in an acting capacity. According to The Mooknayak's report, this change came after Professor Avlendra Kumar Thakur gave up the additional charge of the post.

The controversy began in the last week of September 2026, when some social media posts linked to the registrar's name went viral. They questioned the reservation system, and one post set being Dalit against merit. The institute began an inquiry after complaints from some teachers and rights activists, and Director Amit Patra had said action would be taken if the allegations were proved.

On 5 November an FIR was filed against Thakur at the SC/ST police station in Patna on a written complaint by Congress leader Aditya Kumar Paswan. He is accused of hurting the feelings of Dalits, insulting the spirit of the Constitution and spreading caste hatred. Thakur says the posts are fake or have been tampered with, and that someone made a fake ID in his name on Facebook or LinkedIn. The allegations have not yet been proved.

Paswan called the change a step in favour of constitutional values. Nagsen Sonare, president of an Ambedkarite engineers' organisation, said action was delayed despite the complaints. On social media, some of Thakur's supporters are calling the FIR wrong.
nazar: In institutions like the IITs, Dalit and backward-caste students already put up with taunts of being 'quota students', and when such talk is linked to a high administrative post, the campus atmosphere becomes even heavier. Just changing the charge is not enough; the inquiry must be quick and transparent, so that if the posts are fake that is made clear, and if they are real, accountability is fixed.
sawal: The registrar's chair has changed, but when will the inquiry report come out?
ref: SC/ST police station
Special police stations set up for cases of atrocities against Scheduled Castes and Tribes. Every district in Bihar has one.
Additional charge
When an officer is temporarily given the work of another post along with their own.

h: Baby dies of cold in a Khan Younis tent
dek: The first death as winter sets in over flood-soaked Gaza; more than 50 countries have asked Israel to stop blocking relief supplies.
body: In Khan Younis in southern Gaza, nine-month-old Kanaan Ahmed Raqeeq died of cold during the night in his family's tent. According to his father, Ahmed Raqeeq, when they woke in the morning the baby's skin had turned blue; they took him to Nasser Hospital, but by then it was too late. Mahmoud Basal, spokesperson for Gaza's Civil Defence, also confirmed the death from cold.

This week's heavy rain flooded thousands of tents. The day after the floods, a sand dune slid onto tents, killing five people, including three children. According to the UN humanitarian agency OCHA, 26,000 families had been affected by the storms as of 8 November, and about 65 per cent of Gaza's population is still living in tents or makeshift shelters.

More than 50 countries and organisations, led by Britain, Qatar and Jordan, have demanded that Israel immediately let in shelter, fuel, water, sanitation supplies and medicines, because people face the danger of cold, respiratory illness and diseases spread by dirty water. The US-led 'Board of Peace' and UN relief chief Tom Fletcher have also criticised Israeli restrictions.

Israel's caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says 91,000 tents have been sent and that Hamas is responsible for all the suffering. UNICEF spokesperson James Elder warned that real winter is still weeks away.
nazar: In Gaza, death now comes not only from bombs but also from cold and from relief supplies held back. India calls itself the voice of the Global South; people here too should ask how clear its voice is on the demand to deliver basics like tents, fuel and medicine.
sawal: If 91,000 tents arrived, why did Kanaan die of cold?
ref: OCHA
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. It records relief figures and needs in areas of war and disaster.
Board of Peace
An international body set up at the initiative of the United States after the Gaza ceasefire, tasked with overseeing Gaza's reconstruction and administration.

h: Villagers in Pokhari march in anger over bear attacks
dek: After an eleven-day relay hunger strike, hundreds of people in Pokhari took to the streets, demanding changes to the wildlife law and full compensation.
body: On Thursday, hundreds of villagers in Pokhari tehsil of Chamoli district held a 'jan-aakrosh' (public anger) rally against repeated bear attacks and the deaths of their cattle. The procession went from Gol Market near the Pokhari bus stand to Vinayakdhar Tower and ended with a meeting at the Vinayakdhar junction. All along the way there were slogans against the government, the administration and the forest department.

The movement began on 2 November with an indefinite relay hunger strike at the tehsil headquarters. On the eleventh day, on the assurance of Rajan Suman, DFO of the Kedarnath Wildlife Division, the villagers paused the hunger strike for ten days. The DFO has said he will write to the state government for permission to kill the attacking bears in the affected villages, and will add more cages and forest staff. Five lakh rupees (500,000) has been sanctioned from the Chief Minister's Relief Fund for a woman from Pav village who was injured in a bear attack a year ago.

Badrinath MLA Lakhpat Singh Butola also came to the protest. He alleges that wild animals caught in other places are released in the hills. On 3 September in Sideli village, two women died after falling from a rock while trying to escape a bear. According to the report, since then there have been 13 incidents of bear attacks or cowsheds being broken into in several villages, including Kandai Chandrashila, Raduwa, Jaurasi and Kimotha.
nazar: In the hills, conflict between people and wildlife is now an everyday question for lives that depend on farming and livestock, and the heaviest price is paid by the women who bring in grass and firewood. Compensation comes late and is small, while migration is already emptying the villages. The answer lies not only in permission to kill bears, but in protecting villages, faster compensation and an honest look at the worsening state of the forests.
sawal: What can the forest department achieve in a ten-day reprieve?
ref: Human-wildlife conflict
Clashes between wild animals and people that cause loss of crops, livestock and lives. In Uttarakhand, bears, leopards and elephants are major causes.
Relay hunger strike
A form of protest in which protesters take turns going on hunger strike for a fixed time, so that the movement can go on longer.
ask: Change the wildlife protection law, pay full compensation for losses

h: Farmers sit in protest at the Dalmia sugar mill gate in Nigohi
dek: On the first day of the crushing season, farmers in Shahjahanpur blocked the way for sugarcane carts, handed over a memorandum of 14 demands and warned they would stop the weighing.
body: The crushing season at the Dalmia sugar mill in Nigohi, Shahjahanpur, began on Wednesday, and on the same day farmers began a sit-in at the mill gate. Led by Satyam Bhadauria and Ashish Bhadauria of Dhakia Tiwari village, the farmers arrived at around ten in the morning and blocked both routes used by the sugarcane carts. A long line of trolleys built up on the road.

The farmers handed over a memorandum of 14 demands. These include a bonus of 200 rupees a quintal in line with rising sugar prices, a fix for the traffic jams caused by sugarcane vehicles, street lights and CCTV cameras on the road, and an end to the dirty water and black ash that come out of the mill.

During the talks, an argument between cane general manager Ashish Bansal and the farmers turned into pushing and shoving, which station in-charge Rajeev Tomar brought under control. Later MLA Salona Kushwaha arrived with mill officials and called the demands fair. The general manager promised to sort out the problems within a week, after which one group ended its sit-in.

A second group, led by social worker Satyapal Saxena, held firm on the remaining demands, including the bonus, and said it would not let the cane be weighed until there was a solution. Youth Congress workers also handed over a memorandum in support.
nazar: When sugar prices rise, the profit goes to the mill, the cane price stays where it is, and the dust, the jams and the black ash fall to the farmer and the village. From Shamli to Shahjahanpur, protests across the cane belt of western UP and Rohilkhand bear witness to this imbalance. A one-week promise will mean something only if it is in writing and gives a clear answer on the bonus.
sawal: Sugar got dearer. What did the cane farmer get?
ref: Crushing season
The season for sugar mills, usually November to April, when they buy sugarcane and crush it. Farmers raise their demands right at the start of the season.
Cane slip and weighing
The mill gives farmers a slip and weighs their cane on a fixed day. Stopping the weighing is strong pressure from farmers, because the mill cannot run without it.
ask: Give a bonus of 200 rupees a quintal for the higher sugar prices

h: Aishbagh Janata Quarters: women demand a home for a home
dek: The housing board gave a final notice to vacate by 13 November, and five women swallowed poison during the protest.
body: On Thursday, during a protest against plans to empty and demolish the Janata Quarters in Bhopal's Aishbagh area, five women swallowed a poisonous substance. All five have been admitted to Hamidia Hospital. According to the report, two of them are in a serious condition.

The Madhya Pradesh Housing Board has called the buildings badly dilapidated and issued a final notice asking residents to fully vacate their homes and remove their belongings by 13 November. Demolition is planned from 14 November and the administration has finished its preparations. The municipal corporation had declared these buildings dangerous back in May 2016, yet many families went on living here.

The colony has about 600 homes. By the board's records, only about 110 families are original allottees, and it treats the rest as unauthorised occupants. Since the notice came, residents have put up posters and held protests with a single demand: a home for a home. Their question is where they can go with their children and families at such short notice.
The report does not mention any government plan for rehabilitation or for homes elsewhere, nor any statement from an official.
nazar: Moving people out of a crumbling building can be a way to save lives. But stamping it dangerous, sitting silent for ten years and then giving a few days' notice is eviction, not safety. The families called 'unauthorised' are also the city's workers and poor, with no other roof to go to. That five women ended up in hospital shows how much despair a bulldozer brings when there is no rehabilitation.
sawal: Before 600 homes are pulled down, how many families got a new roof?
ref: Janata Quarters
Cheap housing built by the state housing board for low-income families. In many of these ageing quarters, tenants and other families now live alongside the original allottees.
A home for a home
A common demand of movements against eviction: that no home be demolished until the people living there have first been given another one.
ask: A home for a home: resettle people before demolishing

h: "Let us go home": displaced people to rally in Imphal on 22 November
dek: Seven groups of families who have lived in relief camps for nearly four years have come together to demand resettlement in their own villages.
body: Displaced Meitei families living in relief camps across the Manipur valley will hold a joint rally in Imphal on 22 November. Its slogan is "Let us go home". The apex committee of displaced Meiteis announced this at the Manipur Press Club. The committee is made up of seven organisations, including groups of people uprooted from Churachandpur, Moreh, Torbung, Imphal East and Kangpokpi, and the Mandop Yumpham relief camp.

The rally will start from Thau Ground in Thangmeiband and reach Khuman Lampak, where a public meeting will be held. According to Laishangthem Brojendro Meitei, the committee's spokesperson and general secretary of the Meitei Council Moreh, children and the elderly will also take part. The meeting will pass a resolution for resettlement in the original villages and hand it to the government.

The committee says people have been uprooted for nearly four years, since the violence began on 3 May 2023, and the financial help they get is not enough even for daily needs. Brojendro said all three, the Biren Singh government, President's Rule and the current Khemchand government, had failed at resettlement. He alleged that the Centre is paying no attention to this long humanitarian crisis and that armed groups have a free hand. He appealed to people in the valley to stop work on the day of the rally and stand with them.
nazar: In Manipur, thousands of people, Meitei and Kuki-Zo alike, have been in camps for three and a half years, and "normal conditions" mean nothing to them. The demand to go home belongs not to one community but to the whole state. It will be met only when trust is built on both sides along with security; a demand for military action alone can also open new rifts.
sawal: Who will answer for the schooling of children growing up in the camps?
ref: IDP
Internally displaced people: those forced from their homes by violence or disaster, but still within the country's borders.
Khuman Lampak
A large sports complex in Imphal, where big public meetings and rallies are often held.
ask: Resettle displaced people in their original villages

h: Adivasi farmers in Narmada's Sagbara hold out for forest land titles
dek: The minister announced titles for 450 people, but farmers in Khopi village say the forest department is holding back their rights.
body: In the Sagbara area of Gujarat's Narmada district, the land rights dispute of Adivasi (indigenous) farmers has not been settled. These farmers are asking for title deeds to the forest land they have farmed for years. According to the report, they are preparing to protest again.

Tribal Affairs Minister Naresh Patel has announced that titles for 450 people are ready, and that this is not a one-time job but an ongoing one. He said the forest and revenue departments and the Gir Foundation are also involved, and that villages where there has been a struggle over land will not be left out. Genuine farmers will keep getting titles in future too.

MP Mansukh Vasava went to Khopi village and spoke with the farmers. He alleged that forest department staff do not want to give land to Khopi's farmers. He said that Adivasis who have tilled a piece of land for twenty years have a right to it. He also warned that mistakes in the satellite survey could leave many farmers out of the papers, and asked the farmers to stay united.
It is not yet clear what the next step will be between the farmers and the officials.
nazar: The Forest Rights Act is nearly twenty years old, yet Adivasis still have to sit in protest for the papers to land they have tilled themselves. Handouts of titles are announced, but before satellite images and forest department files, the village's testimony and the gram sabha's decision count for little. Giving people their rights is not a favour; it is a legal duty.
sawal: Why does Khopi's twenty years of farming not show up in the satellite survey?
ref: Sanad / title deed
A document given under the Forest Rights Act 2006 that recognises an Adivasi family's right to the forest land it farms.
Forest Rights Act
A 2006 law under which Adivasis who were tilling forest land before 13 December 2005 get individual and community rights; claims start at the gram sabha (village assembly).
ask: Give title deeds for forest land tilled for years

h: Hyderabad's gig workers win their fight: rules from 14 November
dek: Delivery and cab workers will hold their own rally that day; the union says a demand of many years has finally reached the point of action.
body: According to Shaik Salauddin, founder president of the Telangana Gig and Platform Workers Union, the rules and the welfare board under the state's law for gig workers will be formally notified on 14 November. Rahul Gandhi is expected to visit Hyderabad for the occasion.

Salauddin said workers will hold a small rally of their own that day, with no role for any party. He said the union raised this demand for years with both the Centre and the state, and only now is the law in a position to take effect on the ground. The event will be held near the Hyderabad International Convention Centre, where delivery workers, cab drivers and other platform workers will speak directly. Ministers Ponnam Prabhakar and Gaddam Vivek Venkatswamy inspected the venue.

According to the union, the state government has already paid 5 lakh rupees each to the families of eight gig workers killed in road accidents, and four more cases are in process. The Telangana Platform-Based Gig Workers (Registration, Social Security and Welfare) Act, 2026 was passed this year and has been in force since 2 June.
nazar: Gig workers have so far been kept out of workers' rights by being called "partners". Telangana's law is an attempt to break that thinking, and it is the result of long pressure from the union, not anyone's kindness. The real test will be how much of a voice workers have on the board, and whether companies actually pay their share.
sawal: Will the welfare board be able to collect the set contribution from companies?
ref: Gig workers
People who work for app-based companies and are paid per task, such as delivery workers and cab drivers, but whom the company does not treat as its employees.
Welfare board
A body set up under the law that registers workers and uses contributions taken from companies to run schemes such as insurance and accident compensation.
ask: Full social security for gig and platform workers

h: A tank dry for eight years, 700 tap connections on paper
dek: In Lakhanpur village in Prayagraj, a 1.3 lakh litre water tank was built and pipes reached the homes, but not a single drop has ever come from the taps.
body: Lakhanpur village in Shankargarh block of Prayagraj district is home to about 2,200 people. According to Khabar Lahariya's report, a tall water tank of about 1,30,000 litres was put up here about eight years ago, so that tap water would reach homes in Lakhanpur and nearby. When the tank and pipeline were built, connections were fitted to every house too, but water never came through those taps.

Santosh from the village says the online records of the Jal Jeevan Mission show about 700 homes in the village as connected. On the ground, people depend on hand pumps, wells and private borewells, and the village hand pump is also waiting to be repaired. According to Rani, the solar-powered tank works only when the sun is out, and despite repeated complaints nothing has been fixed.

Village head Ramjatan says the scheme was for the whole panchayat, which covers Barwa and Bhauthi along with Lakhanpur. He says the connections were made but no water came, and it seems the budget was spent without any result. For now, five solar tanks set up from the MP's fund are the main support, and in summer even the hand pumps give up.

Jal Nigam junior engineer Niranjan Verma told the reporter that under the old system five borewells were dug to fill the tank, but none gave enough water. Now a new survey has been done under the Jal Jeevan Mission, and the plan is to bring water from the Yamuna to fill the tank. He also said villagers will not be charged a water bill until supply begins.

The report cites the Central Ground Water Board's district report, which says the ground in the Shankargarh area has layers of sandstone and hard rock, where groundwater depends on the season, the depth of the borewell and cracks in the rock. In other words, the first check should have been whether the source had any water at all, and only then should the tank and pipes have been laid.
nazar: The promise of a tap in every home looks complete in the figures, because connections are counted, not water. Lakhanpur shows that when a scheme is built without checking the groundwater, the money reaches the contractor and the thirst stays in the village. In the rocky areas bordering Bundelkhand, the burden falls most heavily on women, who make round after round to the hand pump and the well.
Now there is a new plan to bring water from the Yamuna. The question is who will answer for the last failure, and whether this time the work will be done after asking the villagers.
sawal: In a village with 700 connections, whose register does the water flow in?
ref: Jal Jeevan Mission
A central government scheme started in 2019 that aims to bring piped drinking water to every rural home.
Its progress is often measured by the number of connections given, not by actual supply.
Central Ground Water Board
A body under the Ministry of Jal Shakti that surveys and assesses groundwater across the country.
Its district reports show how much water can be found in the rocks of each area.

h: Hamlets seventy years old and still no road: children go to the DM's office
dek: About 70 children from two hamlets of Mahoba's Gyodi panchayat, fed up with a muddy path, raised slogans and submitted a petition for a road.
body: Two majras (hamlets) of Gyodi gram panchayat in Uttar Pradesh's Mahoba district, Siddhandera and Ilahipura, are just 400-500 metres from the main Gyodi-Khanna Chak road. But in the rains this short distance turns into a journey of hours. According to Khabar Lahariya's report, only a three to four metre wide dirt path leads to these settlements. It is usable in summer, but as soon as the rains start it sinks under mud and water.

Villagers say Siddhandera has been settled for about 70 years and nearby Shankardera for about 60, yet a proper road was never built. About 180 people live in Ilahipura and Siddhandera together, and about 250 in Shankardera. Madhu says taking a sick person out is the hardest thing, and according to Sheela, the path has filled up like this in the rains for fifteen years.

Children are hit hardest. According to the report, about 70 children from Siddhandera and around cross mud and water to get to school. Pawan Kumar, a teacher at Siddhandera Upper Primary School, says 26 children are enrolled at the school and on rainy days many simply cannot come. Villagers say the children of Shankardera had not been able to go to school for about ten days.

Worn out, about 70 children and villagers went to the District Magistrate's office on 24 August, raised slogans and handed in a written petition for a road. SDM Shivdhyan Pandey said a revenue team had been sent to the spot and a solution would be found after talking to the BDO and the panchayat ADO. Basic Education Officer Rahul Mishra said he would go and see the path himself.

According to village head Siddhnarayan, the road has been included in the plan, but work will start only after approval and once the process moves forward. So for now the children have a promise in hand, and the same dirt path until the next rains.
nazar: The Right to Education Act sets the distance to school, but not the state of the path. Such settlements and hamlets, half a kilometre from the main road, often belong to landless, Dalit or nomadic families, whose voice sits at the very bottom of the panchayat's list of priorities.
Here the children did what decades of petitions by adults could not: they got officials to come to the spot. Now we will see whether the promise turns into a proper road or into a file.
sawal: Why could 400 metres of road not be built in seventy years?
ref: Majra
A small hamlet or settlement set apart from a revenue village or gram panchayat.
In Uttar Pradesh, many majras are left behind the main village in panchayat schemes.
Basic Education Officer
The officer in charge of government primary and upper primary schools in a district.
Enrolment, attendance and facilities in schools are their responsibility.

h: A farm worker died in a thresher, his file has been stuck for 18 months
dek: Sumit of Beriakhedi village in Rajgarh died while working on a farm, but the compensation under a government scheme is still moving between offices.
body: In March 2025, Sumit, the son of farm labourer Purushottam of Beriakhedi village in Madhya Pradesh's Rajgarh district, was caught in a thresher while threshing wheat and died. According to Ground Report, a year and a half later the family has still not received money under the Mukhyamantri Krishak Jeevan Kalyan Yojana (the Chief Minister's farmer welfare scheme), which provides Rs 4 lakh for a death in an accident during farm work and Rs 4,000 for the funeral.

The paper trail has been long. A merg (unnatural death report) was registered on 16 March 2025, and the family applied with that report. In November 2025 the Collector's office asked for the FIR papers, which the tehsil sent again. According to panchayat secretary Omprakash Sharma, the case is pending at the Collector's office. Sarpanch Kamal Panwar says he spoke to the Collector three times: first he was told the papers were incomplete, then that the file had been sent to the Mandi Board.

The farm owner, Sonu Meena, faces a case of death by negligence under Section 106 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, and a chargesheet has been filed. According to him, the thresher's top cover was off and Sumit had climbed up to cover it. According to Deputy Collector Nidhi Bhardwaj, the case is not known to her.

According to figures from the Collector's office, 62 cases under the scheme came up in the district between 1 January 2024 and 9 October 2026. 37 were sanctioned, but 15 of those families have not been paid, 12 were rejected and 12 are still in process.

The report cites a study by Dr L.P. Gite, formerly of the Central Institute of Agricultural Engineering, Bhopal, which found that about 14 percent of accidents involving farm machines are caused by threshers. According to mechanics, many threshers are locally made and uncertified, while the Indian standard requires a chute at least 90 centimetres long and iron guards on rotating parts.
nazar: A farm labourer has no land, and no paper that records his work. Even after his death, his family goes round and round between the merg, the FIR, the postmortem and the Mandi Board. A relief scheme is relief only when it arrives on time; otherwise it becomes one more test for a poor family.

The second question is about the machines. As long as threshers without guards keep running in the fields and the burden of safety stays on the worker, such accidents will go on being treated as 'part' of farming.
sawal: If the cause of death was clear, where was the approval stuck for 18 months?
ref: Merg
In Madhya Pradesh, the first police record of an unnatural or suspicious death.
Only after its inquiry is it decided whether an FIR will be registered.
Mukhyamantri Krishak Jeevan Kalyan Yojana
A Madhya Pradesh government scheme that gives financial help to a farmer or labourer hurt in an accident during farm work.
A death brings Rs 4 lakh, and the payment is made through the Mandi Board.
photo_note: Symbolic image: women gleaning leftover ears of grain in a field, by Jean-François Millet.

h: Straightened rivers, drying land: how can Germany hold on to its water?
dek: A DW documentary travels through three German states to ask how far it is possible to give rivers back their room in a time of falling groundwater and dry soil.
body: Germany is usually seen as a green, rainy country. But this DW documentary, which came out on YouTube on 22 September 2026, shows a different picture: falling groundwater, dry soil and temperatures that keep climbing. The film's basic question is simple: how can more water be kept in the ground in the years to come?

To find an answer, the film goes to three German states and meets four kinds of people: scientists, farmers, environmental groups and politicians. Each has their own worry about water, and their own calculation too. According to the film's description, the clash of these calculations is its real story.

It takes three rivers as examples: the Unstrut, the Mulde and the Elbe. Like many rivers in Europe, these too were straightened over past centuries in the name of farming, shipping and flood protection; their banks were hardened and their floodplains turned into fields and settlements. The film shows that the price of this decades-old work is being paid now, because a straight river carries water away fast and the land gets no time to soak it up.

The documentary explains why floodplains matter. These plains give extra water room to spread during floods, refill the groundwater and become stores of drinking water. With the risk of both drought and flood rising, they are seen as an essential tool for adapting to the climate.

That is why plans are under way in many places to return rivers to a natural form, which in English is called renaturalisation. The film shows the chances these projects offer and also the conflicts they cause. The land to be given back to the river often has a farmer's crop standing on it, and the pull between nature conservation, farming and political interests is plain to see.

The film offers no easy solution. It records that water is no longer just a matter of engineering, but a matter of deciding whose land it is and what it will be used for. Even in a rich industrial country, that decision is not easy.
nazar: For India this film is like a mirror. Here too riverbanks are being paved, colonies and riverfronts are coming up on floodplains, and big schemes like river-linking treat water as an engineering game. From Punjab to Marathwada groundwater is falling, and the first blow lands on small farmers, farm workers and the women who carry water.

Germany at least is debating whether to give the river back its place. Here, it is usually poor settlements that are cleared from the floodplains of the Yamuna or the Mithi, while big buildings stay standing. Giving the river room is necessary, but why should only the weakest pay the price?
sawal: Who, in the end, are the Yamuna's floodplains cleared for?
ref: Floodplain
The low land on either side of a river over which floodwater spreads. It holds back water, refills groundwater and softens the force of floods.
River renaturalisation
The effort to give a straightened, paved river back its winding course, open banks and floodplains.

h: A celebration for a brother's birth, the silent witness of three sisters
dek: The fourth instalment of Mrinal Pande's autobiography records the worth of daughters in a Kumaon household, and the stubbornness of memory.
body: The fourth instalment of Mrinal Pande's autobiography Bhakhai Akath Katha Birtant (Telling the Untold Story), being serialised on Janaki Pul, begins with a birth. On the first of September, at her mother's family home in Almora, the family's only son, Mickey, is born, and relatives rejoice that the line has at last got an heir. The writer remembers that these same people had mocked her mother again and again for giving birth to three daughters.

Inside the instalment is an inner voice that the writer calls the yaksha. It says nothing; it just keeps a record of everything. This is the axis of the prose: the humiliation that passed without a sound in the house kept piling up in memory. According to the editorial note, the writer's mother, the well-known storyteller Shivani, is present throughout in the background of this story.

Around 1956 the family returns from Lucknow to Nainital. A Bharatanatyam teacher offers to send the girl to Kalakshetra, but her father refuses, saying the daughters of his house do not dance on stage. In return comes a promise that the girls will study up to university. Her elder sister Binu, who has become half a mother to her younger sister, asks whether she too will be sent.

In the house there is the grandmother, the widowed aunt Tara Didi who gives blunt advice on restraint and modesty, and a midwife and servants. Horoscopes are kept in a cloth bundle, and a daughter's horoscope comes out only at the time of marriage. An astrologer calls the writer free-thinking and outspoken, yet a match is fixed, and at her grandfather's house in Allahabad she meets her future husband.

The instalment ends in fragments: refugees passing on the road, the grandmother's worn gold bangles, a funeral bier on its way to the cremation ground, a blind beggar. The writer keeps these like raw clay that will later be given shape by language.
nazar: The custom of beating a plate to celebrate a son's birth and keeping quiet over a daughter's is not just Kumaon's but the whole country's, and today's sex ratio figures show this memory has not passed. Pande's prose turns it not into a complaint but into a record. If even in an educated, literary household a daughter could not go on stage, think how many doors must have stayed shut for girls from Dalit, Adivasi or poor homes.
sawal: Why were daughters' horoscopes kept shut away in a bundle?
ref: Shivani
The popular Hindi storyteller Gaura Pant 'Shivani' (1923-2003), whose stories centred on Kumaon society and the lives of women. Mrinal Pande is her daughter.
Kalakshetra
The dance and arts institution founded by Rukmini Devi Arundale in Madras in 1936, which became a major centre for teaching Bharatanatyam.

h: A first collection with a clear stand and sharp images
dek: Yatish Kumar's review of Amit Upmanyu's poetry collection Atirikt Shunya calls it a bridge between memory and reality.
body: On Hindwi's Bela, Yatish Kumar reads Atirikt Shunya (Extra Zero), the first collection by Amit Upmanyu, a poet of the new generation. His first remark plays on the title itself: nothing in these poems is extra, they hit the target directly, and according to the reviewer, piercing the reader is poetry's basic job.

The review's main argument is about the poet's clear stand. Citing a conversation with Kumar Ambuj, Yatish Kumar says a poet should know their place and their ideology. In his view, a poet's mind should not just be a flowing stream; it should also be a stone that can turn the stream's course.

The central tension of the collection lies between restlessness inside and wandering outside. The reviewer says the climb here from everyday speech to philosophy is so smooth that the reader does not notice it. Images from myth, science and technology walk side by side, and pairs like city and forest, human and animal, displacement and shelter keep coming back. One image about corruption in the bureaucracy struck him as especially deadly.

The praise is not blind. Yatish Kumar admits that some poems did not reach him, and in a poem about the pandemic a sudden change of tone stops him from feeling the pain. He also warns that a reader who gets stuck on single lines may lose the thread of the whole poem.

In the end he lists the collection's strengths: dark truths, social contradictions, fresh images, restrained feeling, avoidance of flat statement, and metaphors for the pressures of the age of capital. Drawing on the views of Pawan Karan and Rajesh Joshi, he sees it as an important knock on the door of contemporary Hindi poetry.
nazar: In Hindi, first collections are often either drowned in friendly praise or go unnoticed. This review at least names the weak poems, which is the first condition of honest criticism. And if a new poet can write about displacement, a corrupt system and the pressure of capital without sloganeering, that matters at a time when the pressure to strip poetry of a political stand has grown.
sawal: Should a poet's mind be a stone too, not just a stream?
ref: Bela
Hindwi's prose platform, which publishes reviews, memoirs, diaries and literary notes.
Sapatbayani
Saying something in a poem as a plain statement, without image or tension, which critics often see as a weakness.

h: The classroom pushed him away from poetry, the library brought him back
dek: On Bela, Shachindra Arya remembers how he found his way to poetry through rote learning and closed departments.
body: This memoir by poet and prose writer Shachindra Arya begins with a simple question to which he has no simple answer. He does not remember any one day or event when he came to poetry; memories come like pictures laid one over another. He also admits that he has not been able to write lately, and perhaps that is why the question came up.

At school, poetry meant explanation with context and memorising figures of speech. Nobody cared about meaning, and the writer says this method pushed many children away from poetry for good. He could tell old metrical poetry from new prose-like poetry by its rhythm, but the idea of inner rhythm made no sense to him then.

At university he did not even choose the paper on modern poetry; he studied media. Outside the syllabus, his support was the Delhi Public Library on Peshwa Road. His real bond was with Muktibodh, and Arya's sharp remark is that the teachers who taught Muktibodh were themselves part of the very structures that poetry was restless against. In the classroom, interpretation is herded down a fixed path and exams reward repeating it.

In his Hindi MA days, with the race for NET, the pressure of money and social background, and teachers who would not let students come close, the writer found himself alone. The first poet he chose for himself was Asad Zaidi. Then came cheap anthologies of representative poems bought at book fairs, including Katyayani and Anamika. The piece ends with 'to be continued', so the story will go on.
nazar: This personal memory is really a case against Hindi departments. Where poetry is turned into a marks machine and teachers keep the door shut, the biggest losers are students who have no books at home: first-generation students from villages and small towns, from Dalit and backward-caste families. The public library is their second university, and it is the first to face budget cuts.
sawal: What did the library give that the Hindi department could not?
ref: Saprasang vyakhya
A method in school and college Hindi exams where the context, setting and meaning of lines of poetry have to be written out in a fixed format.
Muktibodh
Gajanan Madhav Muktibodh (1917-1964), poet of long poems such as Andhere Mein (In the Dark), whose poetry centres on power and the inner struggle of the middle class.

h: War, Gaza and vanished birds: Tishani Doshi's most restless book
dek: According to Yamini Krishnan, Egrets, While War sets everyday things beside violence to show the absurd insistence on living.
body: Tishani Doshi's new poetry collection Egrets, While War is out from HarperCollins India. Writing on Scroll, Yamini Krishnan says she read it abroad while news came in of police crackdowns on protests in Delhi, and it struck her then that Doshi's poetry had never been more necessary.

According to the review, the collection's basic move is to set ordinary household things right next to scenes of hunger, violence and war. The world is falling apart and daily chores go on; this contradiction stings again and again. Birds are the emotional centre of the book: they bring small messages of hope, become other forms of the self, and force us to think about extinction.

Krishnan singles out some poems in particular. A poem about a boat heading towards Gaza uses the myth of the albatross to ask what one boat can do against a siege, and the answer is that even small solidarity matters. The dodo becomes a way to speak of India-Pakistan tensions, and the extinction of the last passenger pigeons is linked to the killing of Palestinians in Gaza. A poem dedicated to Gisèle Pelicot turns an island of missing girls into birds.

The later sections turn to old age, desire in menopause, and memories of a grandmother in Madras and a grandfather in Wales, and there is also satire on rich tech moguls' obsession with living forever. The reviewer has one complaint: the bird images are not always as powerful. Still, her conclusion is that this is Doshi's most existential book, recording not only a list of atrocities but also the daily work of going on living against them.
nazar: English poetry in India is often accused of never looking beyond its own drawing room. Doshi puts Gaza, the streets of Delhi and a rape survivor in one book, and that stands against the silence the mainstream has wrapped itself in over Palestine. Extinct birds and people being wiped out: in this pairing lies a warning that once power decides someone is surplus, making them disappear becomes easy.
sawal: What does the last passenger pigeon tell us about Gaza?
ref: Passenger pigeon
A bird of North America whose numbers once ran into billions. Unchecked hunting drove it fully extinct in 1914.
Gisèle Pelicot
The French woman whose husband drugged her for years and had others rape her. She had the 2024 trial held in open court.

h: Iqbal's stars and the telescope of physics
dek: Dr Intikhab Ulfat looks for scientific curiosity in Iqbal's poetry, but firmly refuses to turn it into prophecy.
body: In the Pakistani magazine The Friday Times, Dr Intikhab Ulfat begins with a comparison: the physicist sees the laws of nature in the stars and the poet sees hope and mystery, but both begin with wonder. His argument is that Iqbal was not a scientist, but he wrote at a time when physics and astronomy were changing fast.

The essay places several of Iqbal's images beside modern science. He links the image of the speck and the sun to the unity of matter and energy, the motion inside things that seem still to the Earth, the solar system and the expanding universe, and the idea of an unfinished cosmos to modern cosmology, with its birth and death of stars.

The essay's real strength is its caution. The writer says again and again that Iqbal did not predict nuclear energy, relativity or life on other planets. For him, stagnation was a philosophical and cultural danger, not a law of nature. There is no need to make Iqbal a scientific prophet; his greatness stands without this inflation.

He explains the sunset in the nazm (poem) Bazm-e-Anjum (The Gathering of Stars) from Bang-e-Dara through the scattering of light in the atmosphere: science explains the mechanism, the poet keeps the wonder alive. He links Iqbal's rejection of astrology to khudi (selfhood) and personal responsibility, and while discussing space travel asks why a society that wants to reach Mars cannot give its own people clean water and education.
Finally, reading Talib-e-Ilm (The Student), Ulfat appeals to Pakistani universities not to keep science and literature in separate boxes, because curiosity lies at the root of both.
nazar: On both sides of the border, there is a growing fondness for 'discovering' modern science in old books and poets, and it often serves nationalist or religious pride. Ulfat's essay is a good answer to this: let the poet stay a poet and let science run on evidence. His question about water and schools applies just as much to India, where schools are closing in Adivasi villages amid celebrations of Chandrayaan.
sawal: How does rejecting astrology connect to Iqbal's khudi?
ref: Bang-e-Dara
Muhammad Iqbal's first Urdu poetry collection (1924), which includes nazms such as Saare Jahan Se Achha and Bazm-e-Anjum.
Khudi
The central idea of Iqbal's philosophy: a person's self-awareness and self-respect, which lead them to action instead of bowing before fate.

h: An ear at the puncture shop that catches fake voices
dek: In Ashar Najmi's story, a puncture repairer catches the lie in doctored voices, but against the noise nobody listens to him.
body: The story Abdul Panchar Banata Hai (Abdul Fixes Punctures) by Ashar Najmi, the well-known Urdu fiction writer and editor of Isbaat, has been published on Sammukh. Abdul Latif mends tyres under a flyover in a nameless city. Above him, on a big digital screen, a famous anchor talks day and night. From the sound of the bubbles rising in the water tub, Latif can tell how old the hole is and how big a patch it will need.

He got this ear at a news studio, where he was a sound engineer. On his last day, the editor told him to turn up the noise behind the slogans so the real words would blur. Latif refused, and was taunted to go do his father's work. Now at the shop, a car owner silences him by calling him 'Abdul' when he points out that the slogans of an open-ground protest sound as if they were recorded in a closed room. A boy on a bicycle also advises him to stick to punctures.

At night in his room, Latif listens to a viral clip in which a hospital doctor is accused of talking about poisoning non-Muslim patients. He catches the splice: the word 'poison' is mechanical, the sound of breathing is missing, and there is a sudden jump in the background noise. In the real recording, the doctor is telling the staff to buy oxygen cylinders from the market with their own money.
The video he posts from an account with fourteen followers reaches almost no one; only abuse comes. Then two boys arrive on a motorcycle and threaten that his shop will be the first to go.

In the end, Latif pulls out the audio cable of the screen at the crossing. In three minutes of silence the crowd stands still, then the police take him away. In the final scene, people stand before the black screen as if waiting for someone to speak again.
nazar: This story shows the most dangerous machine of our time: the doctored clip that turns a Muslim doctor into a monster in a moment, and the crowd for whom the speaker's name matters more than the truth. Latif's skill is buried under his identity, and that happens every day to Muslim craftsmen and workers.

In the age of deepfakes, fact-checkers are often alone and voiceless, while the lie has screens and loudspeakers. The story's sharpest question is this: when the noise stops, does the crowd think, or does it wait for the next noise?
sawal: What might the crowd have heard in those three minutes of silence?
ref: Ashar Najmi
Urdu fiction writer and editor who has published the Urdu magazine Isbaat since 2008. His novel Usne Kaha Tha (2021) is considered the first postmodern novel in Urdu.
Deepfake
A fake voice or video made with artificial intelligence, showing a real person saying something they never said.
